sections.text: I see Thee, infinite in form, with, as it were, faces, eyes and limbs everywhere; no beginning, no middle, no end; O Thou Lord of the Universe, Whose Form is universal!
I see thee with the crown, the sceptre and the discus; a blaze of splendour. Scarce can I gaze on thee, so radiant thou art, glowing like the blazing fire, brilliant as the sun, immeasurable.
Imperishable art Thou, the Sole One worthy to be known, the priceless Treasure-house of the universe, the immortal Guardian of the Life Eternal, the Spirit Everlasting.

We had been discussing chapter 11, Vishwarupadarsha yoga of Cosmic Form. As we have seen so far, in the beginning, Arjuna made the request saying that my delusion is gone now. Out of compassion, you explained to me that you are the source of all beings.
You are the resting place of all beings. Nothing exists which is away from you. Everything I see is the manifestation of you alone.
So now my delusion is gone about what is right and what is wrong. However, I would like to see that form of yours in its totality in one place. In the previous chapters we have seen his prakriti Astada Prakruti.
So you can say you can experience, you are seeing it every day. His Eightfold Prakriti, you are experiencing and seeing every day. But I still cant see it in one place.
I basically see as the plurality what I want to see as one entity. Thats basically what we are all struggling with. Intellectually, we understand what Bhagavad Gita says.
But when it comes to day-to-day life, it is very difficult to comprehend. So Arjuna said, my delusion is gone. I understand, but I want to see it, I want to experience it.
And in response, Bhagavan said that if you wish to, I will show you, but you will not be able to see it from your present way of looking at the world, from your present eyes. You will not be able to see it the way you see the world right now -- it will remain divided. Because right now I see my world as I, an individual, and everything else as individual entities.
If I see it that way, I will never be able to see the unity in them. If I change my perspective and see it from the singularitys point of view, and include myself in it, then Ill be able to see it. Thats you have to change your perspective.
So Ill give you that perspective. Divyam Dadami te Chakshuhu. Ill give you that vision and then you will be able to see.
Having said that, he showed the Swarupa, and Sanjaya was the witness. He confirmed that, yes, Yogeshwara Krishna showed Arjuna his Virat Swarupa. And Sanjaya described on his own what Arjuna saw: Aneka Vaktra Bahu -- many mouths and many hands, as if thousands of suns were blazing in the sky at the same time.
It is so resplendent and difficult to see. He also showed us Arjunas reaction: having seen that, Arjuna -- Pranamya Shirasa Devam -- as soon as he saw who Krishna in his real form is, he basically completely surrendered to him. And then what he said is this.
Now we are discussing from verse 15 onward. As we have discussed before, the Bhagavad Gita is generally in Anushtup Chanda. But these verses are in Trishtup Chanda, because there is more to describe.
So these are much longer verses, with more words packed into each verse. This is beautiful poetry, a prayer describing the nature of the Supreme Being. From Arjunas perspective, when he sees that Swarupa, he sees things which are common to his experiences.
When we go to any other town -- like we went to New York and I say Ill go to Manhattan -- what am I going to say? Im going to see the buildings, 911 memorial, One World Tower, because thats the world I see is what Manhattan is all about. So now what Arjuna sees in that Swarupa is what he is familiar with. He says, pasyami Devan Tava Deva, Deva Sarvantatham Bhuta Visesanga O Deva.
He doesnt say Krishna anymore, but O resplendent Being. I see in your body all the other Devas. In this Puranic culture, we have assigned deities to each force of nature, and those resplendent beings, the Devas -- he said, I see in your body all of them.
Pasyami Devan, Tava Deva Dehe. In your body I see them all. Tatha Bhuta Visesa Sangana, various groups of other beings.
Brahmanam Isam, Kamala, Sanastha -- and I see the Lord Brahma. Both ways. He said, this could mean Lord Brahma, or it could mean Brahma and Isha -- Brahma and Shiva -- Kamala Sanastha sitting on the lotus.
I see the whole creation in you, and I see the Creator himself. You are the creation and you are the creator. I see everything all in one.
Tatahu Rishis Cha Sarva -- and I see all the rishis. Its like everything is flashing through his eyes. Everything he has learned about divinity in this world is flashing at the same time.
And also Uragan Cha Divyan -- and I see also the divine serpents. This is one of the techniques poets use -- to take you to the most sublime level and then bring you all the way down to the lowest of the low. So I see all the divine beings, including the Lord Creator himself, but also all the serpents.
The entire universe, from the lowest of the low to the highest of the high -- I see in your body at one time. And then he says Aneka Bahu Udar Vaktra Netra. Sanjaya has already described that before to Dhritarashtra.
Now Arjuna himself says: I see infinite hands. Bahu -- hands, Udara -- stomachs, Vaktra -- mouths, Netra -- eyes. Pasyami tvam Sarvato Anantarupam: I see you facing everywhere.
He is now realizing that this is not something he will be able to describe. Infinite mouths, infinite hands, infinite eyes. As we have discussed earlier, once you take the space out of our world and keep all the beings lumped as one..
Right now I have two hands and you have two hands. But when you are together there are many hands. All the hands in this world are his hands.
All the legs in this world are his legs. All the mouths in this world are his mouths. He is experiencing that.
But then he says, anywhere I see -- you know, like a 360-degree movie projected all over. You are focused on one side, and what happened to the other side? Still the same movie, just different parts. But we cant describe where that movie starts and where that picture ends.
We actually went to the 9/11 memorial. They have a presentation on three sides. When people enter, they start putting their strollers against those walls as if theyre just walls.
Then someone comes and moves all of them because the movie is going to play on all three sides. Then we are focusing on one wall and realize, oh, there are details Im missing on this side. And then, what about that side? We realized we will never be able to capture all three sides at the same time.
Its beyond my capacity to see all three sides at once. So Arjuna is experiencing something at a much grander scale and says, I will not be able to describe everything that I can see. Pasyami tvam Sarvato Anantarupam -- I see you everywhere with infinite forms.
There is no end to what I see in you. Naantam Namadhyam Napunah Ta Adim -- we have learned this before in previous chapters. Bhagavan himself said: I dont have any beginning, I dont have any end.
I am the resting place of everything. Now Arjuna tells him: Bhagavan, I see you as you are -- no end, no beginning, no origin. Pasyami Vishweshvara Vishwaroopa -- he is accepting the fact that you are the Lord of all the universe, and this is your Vishwaroopa.
This is your infinite form. What Im experiencing now is your real nature: you are beginningless, you have no middle and no end. Wherever we stand is the ever-present.
Whatever we left behind is our past. What we have not yet experienced is our future. But if we experience all of it at the same time, there is no beginning, no end, no past, no future.
So hes seeing everything in his present. You are the Lord of the whole universe and I am seeing your Vishwaroopa. Kiritinam Gadhinam Chakrinam Cha -- here, Arjuna is now recognizing that what hes seeing is the divine form he always perceived as the Lord.
Kiritinam Gadhinam Chakrinam Cha Tejo Rashim Sarvato Diptim Anantam: I see you with the crown, the club, and the discus -- the universal form of Vishnu with his four hands holding a lotus, a club, a discus, and a conch. And then he is wearing the crown. Only one who has complete control of his self can wear the crown.
Vishnu is the only one who has complete control of the self. Therefore he wears the crown, which means he has the authority. We wear the crown temporarily.
Whenever I feel I am in authority, I wear my crown. But that only lasts for a limited period of time. My authority slips away before I even realize.
My authority is like the cardboard crown in a drama. While Im on this drama stage, I have that cardboard crown. As soon as Im off this stage, the crown is gone.
Vishnu carries that authority all the time. Thats why he wears the crown. So he holds the lotus which signifies purity and knowledge.
And then he has a conch to wake you up from your ignorance. If you dont listen to the call for waking up, then he uses his club, the gada, to shape you up. And if you shape up, all well and good.
If not, the chakra will annihilate you, just destroy you. So thats how the creation and maintenance continue. Bhagavan gives you all the chances to shape up.
If you dont shape up, time will take care of you. So Arjuna sees that form as the totality. Kiritinam Gadhinam Chakrinam Cha Tejo Rashim Sarvato Diptim Anantam -- a mass of radiance.
Sarvato Diptim -- blazing everywhere. In the previous verses, Sanjaya says it is like a thousand suns blazing in the sky. Here Arjuna says Tejo Rashim Sarvato Diptim Anantam -- everywhere its blazing.
And what hes seeing is not the light of any sun, but the light of the self, the consciousness, that which illumines everything. Anant Diptim -- infinite teja. So he is experiencing resplendence of the self.
Pasyami tvam Durniriksham Samantha. But it is difficult to see. It is difficult to perceive the light of consciousness itself.
Through the light of my consciousness, I understand everything. I see all these things -- Kiritinam Gadhinam Chakrinam Cha -- the crown, the club, the discus. But seeing the consciousness itself, your splendid being, is difficult to see directly.
From the light of my consciousness, I can describe everything. But describing my consciousness itself is not possible. So Dur Niriksham -- I cannot grasp it.
Dur Niriksham Dipta Anala Arka Dyutim Aprameyam. That light is blazing all around like fire and sun, and its incomprehensible. He comes to the conclusion that what he is seeing is undefinable.
At the same time, whatever I want to see, Ill see in it. In any museum or gallery, we go and look at the pictures. Every visitor will see something different.
Even in our world, we see what we want to see. Well never see the things we do not want to see. As soon as we see something which is not conducive, we will run away from it.
Many years ago, when I first started working on a forensic lab and medical examiners office, the first time I met with them they shared statistics about how many people go through an autopsy, how many people die. And the statistics showed something like one in four persons goes through an autopsy.

Arjuna declares three profound realizations: he sees the Lord everywhere with no beginning, no middle, no end; he sees the radiance that is difficult to gaze upon, glowing like blazing fire, brilliant as the sun, immeasurable; and he recognizes Krishna as Imperishable, the Sole One worthy to be known, the priceless Treasure-house of the universe, the immortal Guardian of the Life Eternal. The vision reveals that what we normally see as limited forms with clear boundaries - a beginning here, an end there - are actually expressions of something without any such limits.
Consider how we normally perceive everything with boundaries: this person started here and will end there, this project has a deadline, this relationship has a history. We carve up reality into manageable pieces. But Arjuna now sees that these boundaries are imposed by our minds, not inherent in reality itself. The crown, scepter, and discus he sees represent complete authority (crown), the power to shape (scepter), and the wheel of time and action (discus) - symbols that Krishna is not merely present in the universe but is its controller, sustainer, and essential nature.
For your practice today, look at something you consider complete - a finished task, a relationship that ended, a chapter of life that closed - and contemplate: Where exactly did it begin? What conditions led to those conditions? Trace backward and notice how the beginning dissolves into endless prior causes. Then trace forward: How does what ended continue to influence the present? See how no beginning, no middle, no end applies even to ordinary experiences. This contemplation can soften the rigid boundaries we place on life events and open us to sensing the continuous, beginningless, endless flow of existence.
